props.title: Troll

sections.content: Troll launched a peculiar chapter in 1980s creature features, blending apartment-complex horror with bizarre fairy tale elements. Director John Carl Buechler, fresh from his effects work on Re-Animator (1985), crafted a distinctly weird vision that influenced later evil-in-the-building films like Demons 2 (1986) and Poltergeist III (1988). The film's greatest legacy might be launching Julia Louis-Dreyfus's career and inadvertently spawning the unrelated cult phenomenon Troll 2 (1990), widely celebrated as "the best worst movie ever made."

sections.content: The mid-1980s saw an explosion of diminutive monster movies, with Gremlins (1984) opening the floodgates. Troll rode this wave alongside Ghoulies (1985), Critters (1986), and Munchies (1987). These films shared a common DNA: tiny terrors, practical effects, and a mix of horror and dark humor. Empire Pictures, under Charles Band's leadership, specialized in these creature features, understanding that practical effects and rubber monsters could deliver profitable entertainment on modest budgets.

What sets Troll apart is its bizarre mythology and ambitious world-building. Unlike its contemporaries like Puppet Master (1989) or Dolls (1987), Troll attempted to create a complex fairy tale universe within the confines of a modern apartment building. The film's transformation sequences, where residents become fantastical creatures, showcase impressive practical effects work that holds up better than many of its contemporaries. sections.content: The film's DNA can be seen in later works like Tales from the Darkside: The Movie (1990) and Wishmaster (1997), where ancient evil entities grant twisted "wishes" with horrific consequences. The apartment setting became a template for contained horror, influencing films like Rosemary's Baby (1968) and Dark Water (2005), where domestic spaces become portals to supernatural terror.
